過去形wasは不適。
lest節の仮定法現在で原形beを用いる。
will beは用いない。
items.translation: 植物園では、珍しいコケが踏み荒らされないよう舗装された歩道から出ないよう来園者に求めています。

items.prompt: Far from (     ) interest in print books, the town's reading festival attracted its largest crowd in ten years.
items.explanation: far from＋動名詞（losing）で「〜するどころか（それどころか逆だ）」。
distractorReasons: Far from losing interestで関心を失うどころか。
前置詞fromの後ろに原形は置けない。
過去分詞は置けない。
to不定詞は置けない。
items.translation: 紙の本への関心を失うどころか、町の読書フェスティバルはここ10年で最大の来場者を集めました。

items.prompt: Please back up your presentation files onto an external drive in the (     ) of a network outage.
items.explanation: in the event of＋名詞で「万が一〜が起きた場合には」。
distractorReasons: aspectは側面。

in the course ofは〜の過程で。

ofは使わない。
forは使わない。
items.translation: 新しいリサイクル回収箱には、製品ラベルに印刷された記号に対応する色分けされたふたが付いています。

items.explanation: 下向きフードと暖色化に加え、さらに深夜の人感センサー減光も導入したという追加説明。
distractorReasons: 前の文を否定していない。
In additionは「さらに・加えて」。
さもないと、ではない。
逆接ではない。

passage.title: Rethinking Nighttime Lighting in Parks
passage.text:
Bright streetlamps have long been installed in urban parks to help pedestrians see footpaths and feel secure after sunset. In recent years, however, ecologists and lighting engineers have pointed out an unintended side effect: unshielded white lamps scatter glare into surrounding trees and ponds, disrupting nocturnal insects, bats, and roosting birds.

When a riverside town decided to replace its aging park lamps, officials initially assumed they had to choose between human safety and wildlife protection. Turning lights off completely made evening joggers uneasy. Yet consultations with lighting specialists revealed a third approach. By fitting hoods that directed light strictly downward and shifting from harsh blue-white LEDs to warmer amber tones, the town could keep paths clearly visible while leaving tree canopies dark. (18), motion sensors dimmed secondary trails late at night when nobody was walking past.

Six months after the upgrade, insect surveys along the riverbank showed a marked recovery in moth diversity compared with brightly lit neighboring streets. Residents also responded positively; many noted that shielded lamps actually made it easier to see obstacles on the ground because (19).

The project demonstrated that environmental care does not always demand giving up public convenience. Often, the real problem lies in wasted energy—in this case, light shining into the sky where no walker needs it. Careful design allowed the park to (20).
passage.translation: 都市の公園では日没後の歩行者の安全のため明るい街灯が設置されてきましたが、近年は覆いのない白い光が周囲の樹木や池に漏れ、夜行性の昆虫やコウモリ、眠る鳥に悪影響を与えることが指摘されています。ある川沿いの町が古い街灯を更新する際、当初は「人の安全か野生生物の保護か」の二択だと思われ、完全消灯には夜間のランナーから不安が出ました。しかし照明の専門家と相談し、光を真下だけに絞るフードを付け、青白いLEDから温かみのある琥珀色に変えることで、樹冠を暗く保ちつつ歩道をはっきり照らす第3の方法が見つかりました。(18)、深夜に人が通らない小道では人感センサーで減光しました。半年後の調査では川辺のガの多様性が回復し、住民からも(19)ため地面の障害物がかえって見やすくなったと好評でした。環境配慮は必ずしも利便性の犠牲を求めるわけではなく、空へ漏れる無駄な光をなくす設計によって公園は(20)ことができました。

ランタン持参の義務はない。
まぶしい光が歩行者の目に直接入らなくなったため。
木を切ったのでは樹冠を暗く保った話と矛盾。
items.translation: 空所(19)の補充。

passage.title: Why Recipes Sometimes Fail at High Altitude
passage.text:
Travelers staying in a mountain cabin two thousand meters above sea level are often puzzled when a familiar family recipe turns out strangely. Spaghetti takes longer to soften in boiling water, while a sponge cake that rises beautifully near the coast may puff up too fast in the oven and then collapse in the middle.

The cause is lower atmospheric pressure. At sea level, the weight of the air above pushes down on a pot of water, keeping molecules in liquid form until the temperature reaches 100 degrees Celsius. High in the mountains, thinner air exerts less pressure, so water begins boiling at around 93 degrees. Turning up the stove flame only produces more steam; it cannot make the boiling water any hotter. (21), foods cooked by boiling simply need extra minutes to finish.

Baking involves the same physics in reverse. Bubbles of steam and gas inside cake batter expand more forcefully when external air pressure is weak. Before the flour and eggs have time to set into a firm structure, the batter stretches too thin and sinks. Experienced mountain bakers compensate by reducing leavening powder slightly and raising oven temperature a little so the structure firms up sooner. (22), adding a spoonful of extra liquid prevents the batter from drying out in thin, dry mountain air.

Understanding these adjustments turns kitchen frustration into a practical science lesson. A recipe written in a coastal city assumes invisible environmental conditions. Once cooks recognize (23), they can adapt their methods confidently wherever they travel.

passage.title: Why Recipes Sometimes Fail at High Altitude
passage.text:
Travelers staying in a mountain cabin two thousand meters above sea level are often puzzled when a familiar family recipe turns out strangely. Spaghetti takes longer to soften in boiling water, while a sponge cake that rises beautifully near the coast may puff up too fast in the oven and then collapse in the middle.

The cause is lower atmospheric pressure. At sea level, the weight of the air above pushes down on a pot of water, keeping molecules in liquid form until the temperature reaches 100 degrees Celsius. High in the mountains, thinner air exerts less pressure, so water begins boiling at around 93 degrees. Turning up the stove flame only produces more steam; it cannot make the boiling water any hotter. (21), foods cooked by boiling simply need extra minutes to finish.

Baking involves the same physics in reverse. Bubbles of steam and gas inside cake batter expand more forcefully when external air pressure is weak. Before the flour and eggs have time to set into a firm structure, the batter stretches too thin and sinks. Experienced mountain bakers compensate by reducing leavening powder slightly and raising oven temperature a little so the structure firms up sooner. (22), adding a spoonful of extra liquid prevents the batter from drying out in thin, dry mountain air.

passage.title: Borrowing Tablets for the Field Survey
passage.text:
From: Mr. Watanabe, Geography Department
To: Fieldwork Group Leaders
Subject: Tablet checkout and offline maps for Thursday

Hello group leaders,
For Thursday's land-use survey around Kawagoe District, each group will receive one school tablet preloaded with our mapping app. Because mobile data reception can be weak near the old canal, you must download your assigned sector's offline map onto the tablet before leaving campus. Come to the geography prep room during Wednesday lunch break to check out your device and complete the download over school Wi-Fi.

During the survey, use the app to mark building types and photograph street signs, but avoid photographing private house nameplates or pedestrians' faces. Each tablet comes with a shoulder strap; whoever is carrying the device must wear the strap at all times when walking near water.

All groups must return to school by 3:45 p.m. so data can be backed up before club activities begin at 4:15 p.m. Do not delete accidental photos in the field—you might erase shared group pins by mistake. We will sort the files together back in the classroom.

Regards,
K. Watanabe
passage.translation: 地理科の渡辺先生からフィールドワーク班長への連絡。木曜の川越地区土地利用調査では地図アプリ入りの学校タブレットを各班1台貸し出す。旧運河付近は電波が弱いことがあるため、出発前に担当区画のオフライン地図をダウンロードしておく必要がある。水曜の昼休みに地理準備室へ来て端末を受け取り、校内Wi-Fiでダウンロードを済ませること。調査中は建物の種類を記録し道路標識を撮影するが、個人宅の表札や歩行者の顔は写さないこと。水辺を歩く際は落下防止のため付属のショルダーストラップを必ず着用すること。4時15分の部活動開始前にデータをバックアップするため午後3時45分までに帰校すること。共有ピンを誤消去する恐れがあるため現地で失敗写真を削除せず、帰校後に教室で一緒に整理する。

passage.title: How Libraries Handle Returned Books Behind the Scenes
passage.text:
When library patrons slip a borrowed novel through a return slot, their part of the transaction takes two seconds. Behind the wall, however, getting thousands of returned items back onto the exact shelves where the next reader can find them is a logistical challenge. Even a book placed two shelves away from its call number is effectively lost until someone spots it during a manual shelf check.

Many large public libraries have adopted radio-frequency identification, or RFID, tags—thin stickers with tiny antennas placed inside book covers—paired with conveyor belts that sort returned items into bins by floor and subject. Automation speeds up check-in and reduces repetitive strain on staff wrists. Yet technology alone has not made human judgment unnecessary.

Machines cannot easily tell whether a picture book has a torn page, whether a travel guide is missing its fold-out map, or whether rain has dampened the corners of a textbook. Staff still inspect items as they come out of the bins, setting aside damaged volumes for tape repair or drying before mildew can spread to neighboring books on the shelf. In addition, librarians watch which topics return in waves—such as gardening in April or tax guides in February—and place popular returns on front display tables rather than sending them straight to distant stacks.

Smaller branch libraries without conveyor systems rely on simple workflow rules instead. Returned books are first arranged in exact order on wheeled carts before anyone walks into the reading room, cutting shelving time in half and keeping aisles clear for visitors. New student assistants are also asked to shelve for only thirty minutes at a stretch, because fatigue sharply increases misplacement mistakes.

Whether a library uses sensor-guided belts or hand-pushed carts, accuracy depends on combining reliable routines with attentive human eyes. A catalog is useful only when the physical book is actually waiting where the screen says it is.

passage.title: Why Escalators Leave One Side Debate Behind
passage.text:
In many busy subway stations, commuters follow an unwritten rule on escalators: stand on one side and leave the other lane clear for people in a hurry. At first glance, this arrangement seems polite and efficient. In recent years, however, transit operators from Tokyo to London have begun asking riders to stand in both lanes and refrain from walking on moving steps.

Safety was the initial concern. Escalator steps are much taller than ordinary stairs, so a single misstep by someone carrying a bag can cause a chain of falls. Yet engineers studying station crowds found a second, surprising problem. When ninety percent of riders prefer to stand, reserving half the escalator for the few who walk leaves the walking lane mostly empty. (18), queues at the bottom grow longer during rush hour.

Field trials confirmed the math. Stations that guided commuters to stand two abreast moved roughly twenty-five percent more people per minute than stations using the stand-and-walk split. Standing evenly also reduced uneven mechanical wear on rollers and chains, because (19).

Changing habits formed over decades takes patience, of course. Clear floor footprints and calm voice reminders work better than scolding posters, helping riders understand that (20).
passage.translation: 多くの混雑する地下鉄駅では、エスカレーターの片側に立ち、急ぐ人のためにもう片側を空ける暗黙の習慣があります。一見礼儀正しく効率的に思えますが、近年は東京からロンドンまで多くの鉄道事業者が、歩かずに両側へ立って乗るよう呼びかけ始めています。最初の理由は安全性で、エスカレーターの段差は通常の階段よりずっと高いため、荷物を持った人が一歩踏み外すだけで連鎖的な転倒につながりかねません。しかし駅の混雑を調べた技術者は2つ目の意外な問題を見つけました。乗客の9割が立ち止まりたいとき、歩く少数のために半分を空けると歩行側の列はスカスカになり、(18)、ラッシュ時には乗り口前の行列が長くなってしまうのです。実証試験でも2列で立ち止まる駅のほうが1分あたり約25％多くの人を運べました。また(19)ため、ローラーやチェーンの偏った摩耗も減りました。長年身についた習慣を変えるには忍耐が要りますが、床の足形表示や穏やかな音声案内によって(20)と理解してもらう取り組みが進んでいます。

passage.title: Why Escalators Leave One Side Debate Behind
passage.text:
In many busy subway stations, commuters follow an unwritten rule on escalators: stand on one side and leave the other lane clear for people in a hurry. At first glance, this arrangement seems polite and efficient. In recent years, however, transit operators from Tokyo to London have begun asking riders to stand in both lanes and refrain from walking on moving steps.

Safety was the initial concern. Escalator steps are much taller than ordinary stairs, so a single misstep by someone carrying a bag can cause a chain of falls. Yet engineers studying station crowds found a second, surprising problem. When ninety percent of riders prefer to stand, reserving half the escalator for the few who walk leaves the walking lane mostly empty. (18), queues at the bottom grow longer during rush hour.

Field trials confirmed the math. Stations that guided commuters to stand two abreast moved roughly twenty-five percent more people per minute than stations using the stand-and-walk split. Standing evenly also reduced uneven mechanical wear on rollers and chains, because (19).

Changing habits formed over decades takes patience, of course. Clear floor footprints and calm voice reminders work better than scolding posters, helping riders understand that (20).

passage.title: Testing Acoustics with Cardboard Models
passage.text:
Before a city spends billions of yen building a concert hall, architects must be confident that a violin played softly on stage will sound warm and clear in the back balcony. Computer simulations have improved dramatically, yet sound waves bouncing off curved balconies, wooden slats, and hundreds of seats interact in ways that pure equations can still misjudge.

To catch acoustic flaws early, specialist teams often build scale models of a proposed hall—typically one-tenth the real size—out of varnished wood, dense cardboard, and miniature velvet chairs. Testing a one-tenth model requires a clever trick of physics. Because every wall and balcony is ten times smaller, engineers play test sounds at ten times their normal pitch so the wavelengths shrink in matching proportion. Tiny microphones placed where audience ears would be record how echoes decay. (21), designers can compare different ceiling angles in an afternoon without pouring a drop of concrete.

Even air inside the model needs adjustment. Ordinary room moisture absorbs ultra-high-frequency sound far faster than real hall air absorbs normal music. Teams therefore pump dry nitrogen into the sealed model or apply mathematical corrections so high notes do not vanish artificially fast. (22), miniature foam figures sit in the seats to imitate how clothed audiences soften reflections.

Once the real hall opens, musicians still fine-tune stage reflectors by ear. Even so, physical scale models provide (23) before construction cranes ever arrive.
passage.translation: 市が何十億円もかけてコンサートホールを建設する前、建築家は舞台上の繊細なバイオリンの音が後方バルコニーまで温かく明瞭に届くか確かめなければなりません。コンピュータ解析は飛躍的に進歩しましたが、曲面のバルコニーや木の格子、何百もの座席で跳ね返る音波の複雑な干渉は数式だけでは見誤ることがあります。そこで専門チームは塗装した木材や厚紙、小さなベルベット椅子で実物の10分の1ほどの縮尺模型を作ります。壁や天井が10分の1の大きさなので、波長も同じ比率で縮むよう通常の10倍の高さの試験音を鳴らし、客席の耳の位置に置いた超小型マイクで残響の減衰を測ります。(21)、コンクリートを1滴も流す前に午後の数時間で天井角度の違いを比較できます。模型内の空気にも工夫が要り、通常の湿気は超高周波音を吸収しすぎるため乾燥窒素を満たすか補正計算を行い、(22)、服を着た観客による音の吸収を再現するため小さな発泡体の人形を座席に並べます。開館後も耳での微調整は行われますが、縮尺模型はクレーンが入る前の段階で(23)を与えてくれます。

passage.title: Guidelines for the Inter-School Science Poster Exchange
passage.text:
From: Ms. Fujita, Science Committee Coordinator
To: Presenting Student Teams
Subject: Poster tube labels and presentation timing for Saturday

Dear student teams,
Twelve high schools will gather in our gymnasium this Saturday for the Prefectural Youth Science Poster Exchange. Please read these practical details carefully so setup goes smoothly in the morning.

Each team has been assigned a numbered display panel measuring 90 centimeters wide by 120 centimeters tall. Bring your printed A0 poster rolled inside a protective tube—do not fold it, as creases cast shadows under the gym spotlights and make small graphs hard to read. We will supply removable paper tape; thumbtacks and strong double-sided tape are prohibited because the panels are rented from the city hall.

To make sure every presenter also gets to view other schools' research, the two-hour session is split into odd-numbered and even-numbered rounds. Odd-numbered teams will stand by their panels for the first hour while even-numbered teams circulate, and then roles will reverse at 11:00 a.m. At least one member of your team must remain at your panel throughout your assigned hour.

Lunch boxes may be eaten in the second-floor cafeteria, not inside the gymnasium.

Best wishes,
R. Fujita
passage.translation: 理科委員会担当の藤田先生から発表生徒チームへの連絡。今週土曜、本校体育館に12校が集まり県青少年科学ポスター交流会を開く。各班には幅90センチ×高さ120センチの番号付き展示パネルが割り当てられる。A0サイズの印刷ポスターは折り目がつくとスポットライトの下で影ができ小さなグラフが読みにくくなるため、折らずに保護筒へ丸めて持参すること。市役所からの借用パネルなので画びょうや強力両面テープは禁止で、剥がせる紙テープを会場で配布する。発表者自身も他校の研究を見られるよう2時間のセッションを奇数・偶数番号で前半後半に分ける。最初の1時間は奇数番号チームがパネル前に立ち偶数チームが見学し、午前11時に交代する。担当の1時間は最低1名がパネル前に残ること。昼食は体育館内ではなく2階食堂でとること。

passage.title: Why Botanical Illustrators Still Draw by Hand
passage.text:
Modern digital cameras can capture every vein on a flower petal in a fraction of a second, complete with accurate color and microscopic sharpness. Given such tools, newcomers to botanical science are often surprised to learn that major herbaria and natural history museums still commission trained artists to draw newly described plant species in pen and ink.

A photograph records a single individual plant at one exact moment—under specific lighting, with whatever insect bite, wilted leaf, or overlapping stem happens to be present that afternoon. Taxonomists naming a species, however, need an image that shows the defining traits shared across healthy specimens, free from distracting accidents. items.prompt: How does a botanical illustrator overcome the focus problem seen in high-magnification photography?
choices: By adjusting microscope focus across layers and drawing all parts clearly with varied line weights.
By flattening every flower with a heavy iron before drawing.
By painting only plants taller than two meters.
By copying older photographs from nineteenth-century books.
items.explanation: 解剖顕微鏡のピントを少しずつ動かして観察し、線の太さを使い分けながら手前から奥まで全ての層を鮮明に描く。
distractorReasons: 第3段落の記述と一致。
重いアイロンで潰すのではない。
2メートル以上の植物限定ではない。
古い写真の模写ではない。
items.translation: 植物画家は高倍率写真で見られるピントの問題をどう克服しますか。

items.prompt: Why do botanists and illustrators work closely together during the pencil-sketch stage?
choices: To choose the most expensive gold frame for an art auction.
To ensure measurements and tiny structural details are scientifically accurate.
Because botanists are not allowed to look through microscopes.
To invent imaginary flowers for science-fiction novels.
items.explanation: ノギスで測った下絵の段階で、微細な毛の角度や茎の鱗片の数など分類上の特徴が科学的に正確か確認し合うため。
distractorReasons: オークション用の額選びではない。
第4段落の共同作業の内容と一致。
植物学者が顕微鏡を見られないとはない。
架空の花の創作ではない。
items.translation: 鉛筆下絵の段階で植物学者と画家が緊密に協力するのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: What sometimes happens while an illustrator is carefully drawing a specimen?
choices: The artist notices distinguishing features that the researcher initially missed.
The plant turns into a different species overnight.
The microscope lens melts from ink fumes.
All photographs of the plant are thrown away.
items.explanation: Sometimes the act of drawing uncovers diagnostic details that the scientist had overlookedとある。
distractorReasons: 研究者が最初のメモで見落としていた識別上の特徴が見つかることがある。
一晩で別種に変わることはない。
インクでレンズが溶けることはない。
写真は生きた色や環境記録として併用される。
items.translation: 画家が標本を丁寧に描いている最中に時々起きることは何ですか。

items.prompt: How does the author view the relationship between photography and hand illustration in botany?
choices: Hand illustration will make field cameras obsolete within five years.
Photography is useful only for amateurs, never for museums.
Both methods have been replaced by verbal descriptions alone.
Each method has distinct strengths that complement the other.
items.explanation: 現地での色や環境を記録する写真と、複雑な立体構造を明快に抽出する線画はライバルではなく互いに補い合うパートナーだとしている。
distractorReasons: カメラが廃れるとは言っていない。
アマチュア専用とは言っていない。
文章だけに置き換わったとはない。
最終段落のpartners rather than rivalsと一致。
items.translation: 筆者は植物学における写真と手描き図の関係をどう捉えていますか。

items.prompt: The coastal road will be widened next spring to (     ) heavy weekend traffic near the ferry terminal.
items.explanation: 週末の激しい交通渋滞を「緩和する・和らげる」ために道路を拡幅するのでrelieve。
distractorReasons: reciteは暗唱する。
resembleは似ている。
relieve heavy trafficで渋滞を緩和する。
recruitは募集する。
items.translation: フェリー乗り場近くの週末の激しい渋滞を緩和するため、来春その海岸道路が拡幅されます。

items.prompt: Even minor cracks in a ceramic teapot can cause it to leak once boiling water makes the clay (     ).
items.explanation: 熱湯によって粘土がわずかに「膨張する」ことで小さなひびから水漏れするexpand。
distractorReasons: expandは熱などで膨張する・広がる。
expireは期限が切れる。
exportは輸出する。
exposeはさらす（他動詞）。
items.translation: 陶器の急須のわずかなひびでも、熱湯で粘土が膨張すると水漏れの原因になることがあります。

items.prompt: Students participating in the debate tournament are expected to back (     ) their claims with reliable statistics.
items.explanation: back up A with Bで「BによってA（主張）を裏づける」。
distractorReasons: back awayは後ずさりする。
back offは手を引く。
back outは（約束などを）取りやめる。
back up claimsで主張を裏づける。
items.translation: ディベート大会に参加する生徒は、信頼できる統計で自らの主張を裏づけることが求められます。

items.prompt: Because the wooden annex lacks central heating, it is used only on a (     ) basis during mild spring and autumn weeks.
items.explanation: 穏やかな春と秋の時期にだけ「季節限定で」使われるon a seasonal basis。
distractorReasons: sensibleは賢明な。
seasonalは季節的な・季節限定の。
stubbornは頑固な。
scarceは乏しい。
items.translation: その木造の別棟には中央暖房がないため、穏やかな春と秋の週に限って季節的に使われています。

items.prompt: The town's disaster map is updated every two years in (     ) with neighborhood fire captains.
items.explanation: in consultation with ... で「…と協議のうえ・相談しながら」。
distractorReasons: contradictionは矛盾。
consumptionは消費。
in consultation withで〜と相談して。
concentrationは集中。
items.translation: 町の防災マップは、地区の消防団長たちと協議しながら2年ごとに更新されています。

items.prompt: At first the two painters worked in very different styles, yet over time they had a strong mutual (     ) on each other.
items.explanation: 時が経つにつれ互いに強い「影響」を与え合ったmutual influence on each other。
distractorReasons: instanceは実例。
innocenceは無実・純真。
ignoranceは無知。
have an influence onで〜に影響を与える。
items.translation: 当初その2人の画家はまったく異なる作風でしたが、やがて互いに強い影響を与え合いました。

items.prompt: The cycling helmet feels remarkably light, yet its inner foam is dense enough to (     ) sudden impacts.
items.explanation: 軽いが内側のフォームが急な衝撃を「吸収する」のに十分な密度があるabsorb。
distractorReasons: absorb impactsで衝撃を吸収する。
admireは感心する。
accuseは非難する。
appointは任命する。
items.translation: その自転車用ヘルメットは驚くほど軽く感じますが、内側の発泡材は急な衝撃を吸収するのに十分な密度があります。

items.prompt: With snowstorms approaching the pass, truck drivers had no (     ) but to wait at the service area overnight.
items.explanation: have no alternative but to doで「〜する以外に選択肢がない・〜せざるを得ない」。
distractorReasons: ambitionは野心。
have no alternative but to waitで待つよりほかない。
allowanceは手当・小遣い。
affectionは愛情。
items.translation: 峠に吹雪が近づいていたため、トラックの運転手たちはサービスエリアで一晩待つほかありませんでした。

items.prompt: The bakery displays ingredient cards in both Japanese and English for the (     ) of international residents.
items.explanation: for the convenience of ... で「…の便宜のために・利用しやすいように」。
distractorReasons: for the convenience ofで〜の利便性のために。
coincidenceは偶然の一致。
conscienceは良心。
competenceは能力。
items.translation: そのパン屋では外国人住民にわかりやすいよう、日本語と英語の両方で原材料カードを表示しています。

items.prompt: Although the new sorting machine works fast, fragile peaches must still be packed (     ) by experienced staff.
items.explanation: 自動選別機は速いが、傷みやすい桃は今も熟練スタッフの「手作業で」箱詰めされるmanually。
distractorReasons: mentallyは精神的に。
mutuallyは相互に。
manuallyは手作業で・手動で。sorting machineと対比。
merelyは単に（packed merely byでは対比の意味が弱い）。
items.translation: 新しい選別機は高速で動きますが、傷みやすい桃は今でも熟練スタッフの手作業で箱詰めしなければなりません。

items.prompt: The documentary was praised for presenting a balanced view rather than being (     ) toward one side.
items.explanation: 一方の側に「偏っている」のではなくバランスの取れた見方を示したbiased toward。
distractorReasons: briefは簡潔な。
blessedは恵まれた。
boundは〜行きの・義務づけられた。
biased towardで〜に偏った。balancedと明確に対比。
items.translation: そのドキュメンタリーは一方に偏ることなく、バランスの取れた視点を示したことで称賛されました。

items.prompt: Please refrain from stepping off the wooden boardwalk lest delicate wetland plants (     ) crushed.
items.explanation: lest＋主語＋(should)＋原形（be）で「〜されないように」。湿原の繊細な植物が踏みつぶされないよう木道から出ない。
distractorReasons: 直説法現在areは用いない。
lest節の仮定法現在で原形beを用いる。
過去形wereは用いない。
will beは用いない。
items.translation: 繊細な湿原植物が踏みつぶされないよう、木道から外へ踏み出さないでください。

items.prompt: Only when she read the diary fifty years later (     ) she realize how hard her grandparents had worked.
items.explanation: Only when ... が文頭に出たことによる主節の倒置。過去時制でrealizeが原形なのでdid。

passage.title: Why Supermarkets Sell "Weather-Marked" Fruit
passage.text:
Shoppers choosing apples or pears in a supermarket often equate smooth, spotless skin with good flavor. As a result, fruit whose skin was lightly scratched by wind-blown twigs or summer hail is frequently rejected by retail buyers, even when the flesh underneath is just as crisp and sweet as top-grade produce.

After an early autumn typhoon scarred nearly forty percent of one orchard town's apple crop, local cooperatives tried a different approach rather than selling the fruit cheaply for juice alone. They packed the apples in clear bags with a small illustrated card explaining how wind marks form on branches and assuring buyers that the inside was unaffected. Supermarkets priced these "weather-marked" bags twenty percent lower than gift-grade fruit. (18), families looking for everyday snacks bought out the first shipment within days.

Follow-up surveys showed an interesting shift in customer attitudes. Shoppers who tasted the discounted apples realized that minor surface marks had no bearing on sweetness or storage life. (19), orchards earned nearly double what juice factories would have paid, helping farmers cover pruning and repair costs after the storm.

Cosmetic standards still matter for formal seasonal gifts, of course. Yet giving honest context at the shelf proved that (20).
passage.translation: スーパーでリンゴや梨を選ぶ買い物客は、傷ひとつない滑らかな皮をおいしさの証と考えがちです。そのため風に揺れた小枝や夏のひょうで皮に薄い擦り傷がついた果物は、果肉の歯ごたえや甘みが一級品と変わらなくても仕入れ段階で敬遠されてきました。ある果樹産地の町で初秋の台風によりリンゴの約4割に傷がついた際、地元農協はジュース原料として安値で手放す代わりに別の方法を試みました。枝で風傷ができる仕組みと中身に問題がないことを絵入りカードで添え、贈答・特秀品より2割安く販売したのです。(18)、日常のおやつを探していた家庭が数日で初回入荷分を買い切りました。追跡調査では客の意識にも変化が見られ、表面の小さな傷は甘さや日持ちに関係ないと実感されました。(19)、農家はジュース工場向けのほぼ2倍の収入を得て嵐の後の剪定や補修費を賄えました。贈答用の見た目基準は残るものの、売り場で正直な背景を伝えたことは(20)と証明しました。

passage.title: Keeping Bus Timetables Readable for Everyone
passage.text:
Public transit agencies pack an impressive amount of data onto a single bus-stop sign: weekday runs, Saturday schedules, holiday exceptions, fare zones, and route branches. For regular commuters who ride the same 7:42 a.m. bus every day, dense columns of tiny numbers soon become familiar. For an occasional rider, an older resident with declining eyesight, or a visitor standing in the rain, however, reading that grid can feel like solving a puzzle.

When a coastal city redesigned its three hundred bus-stop poles, designers began by watching people actually use the signs. Many riders traced rows with a finger because closely spaced lines caused their eyes to jump from the 8:00 row to the 9:00 row. Simply increasing font size was not enough on narrow poles, so the team removed repeated minute labels, grouped departures by morning, midday, and evening bands, and added subtle gray shading to every second row. (21), misreading errors in user tests dropped by more than half.

Equally helpful was replacing text-heavy footnotes—such as "Buses marked with a triangle bypass Harbor Hospital on Sundays"—with a small diagram showing the two route branches visually. Riders grasped where each numbered bus went in seconds rather than hunting for tiny symbols at the bottom of the board. (22), high-contrast black ink on matte yellow-white panels reduced glare under both midday sun and streetlamps.

Digital arrival apps are convenient, yet batteries die and tourists may lack data plans. Treating the humble bus-stop sign as serious information design ensures that (23).
passage.translation: 路線バスの停留所標識には平日・土曜・祝日の時刻や運賃区間、系統の分岐など膨大な情報が詰め込まれています。毎朝同じ7時42分発に乗る常連客には小さな数字の列もじきに見慣れますが、たまに乗る人や視力が落ちてきた高齢者、雨の中で立つ旅行者にはパズルのように感じられます。ある海辺の市が300基のバス停標識を刷新した際、デザイナーが利用者を観察すると、行間が狭いため指でなぞらないと8時台から9時台へ目線がずれる人が多くいました。細い柱では単に文字を大きくするだけでは収まらないため、重複表記を整理して朝・昼・夕の帯に分け、1行おきに薄いグレーの網掛けを入れました。(21)、利用者テストでの読み間違いは半分以下に減りました。また「三角印は日曜に港病院を通過」といった細かい注記を小さな分岐図に置き換えたことで、数秒で行き先が分かるようになりました。(22)、つや消しの淡黄色パネルに高コントラストの黒文字を使ったことで日中の日差しでも夜間の街灯下でも反射が抑えられました。素朴なバス停標識を真剣に設計することは(23)を確実にします。

distractorReasons: さもないと、ではない。

Furthermoreでさらなる視覚的改善点を付け加える。

passage.title: Preparing Exhibits for the Town History Week
passage.text:
From: K. Nagai, Local Archive Volunteer Desk
To: High School History Club Members
Subject: Handling family photos and interview cards on Friday

Dear History Club members,
Thank you for helping set up Friday's exhibition, "Everyday Life Along the Shopping Arcade, 1960–1990," at the civic gallery. Residents have lent us more than sixty original family photographs and shop ledgers, so careful handling during afternoon setup is essential.

Whenever you touch original photographs or paper ledgers, please wear the clean white cotton gloves placed on the worktable. Natural oils from bare fingertips leave invisible marks that slowly turn brown on old silver-gelatin prints. If you need to use your smartphone or write notes with a ballpoint pen, take the gloves off first so ink or screen dust does not transfer onto the items.

Each display case will pair an original object with a short story card based on your club's interviews with shopkeepers. Before placing any card inside a case, check with the lender's consent form in the green binder to confirm whether the resident wished to be named in full or identified only by initials.

Setup runs from 4:00 p.m. to 5:45 p.m.; bottled drinks must stay on the hallway shelf outside the gallery.

Sincerely,
K. Nagai
passage.translation: 地域アーカイブ・ボランティア窓口の永井から高校歴史部員への連絡。金曜の市民ギャラリー展示「商店街の暮らし 1960〜1990」の設営協力へのお礼。住民から60点以上の当時の家族写真や商店の帳簿を借用しているため、午後の設営では慎重な扱いが不可欠。実物の写真や紙の帳簿に触れる際は必ず作業台の清潔な白い綿手袋を着用すること（素手の皮脂は目に見えない跡を残し、古い銀塩写真の上で徐々に茶色く変色するため）。スマートフォンを操作したりボールペンでメモを書いたりする際は、インクや画面の汚れが資料に移らないよう一度手袋を外すこと。各展示ケースには実物資料と店主インタビューに基づく紹介カードを並べるが、ケースに入れる前に緑のバインダーの同意書を確認し、貸出者がフルネーム掲載を希望したかイニシャル表記を希望したか確かめること。設営は午後4時〜5時45分で、ペットボトル飲料はギャラリー外の廊下の棚に置くこと。

items.prompt: What should students do before using a ballpoint pen or smartphone?

passage.title: Preparing Exhibits for the Town History Week
passage.text:
From: K. Nagai, Local Archive Volunteer Desk
To: High School History Club Members
Subject: Handling family photos and interview cards on Friday

Dear History Club members,
Thank you for helping set up Friday's exhibition, "Everyday Life Along the Shopping Arcade, 1960–1990," at the civic gallery. Residents have lent us more than sixty original family photographs and shop ledgers, so careful handling during afternoon setup is essential.

Whenever you touch original photographs or paper ledgers, please wear the clean white cotton gloves placed on the worktable. Natural oils from bare fingertips leave invisible marks that slowly turn brown on old silver-gelatin prints. If you need to use your smartphone or write notes with a ballpoint pen, take the gloves off first so ink or screen dust does not transfer onto the items.

Each display case will pair an original object with a short story card based on your club's interviews with shopkeepers. Before placing any card inside a case, check with the lender's consent form in the green binder to confirm whether the resident wished to be named in full or identified only by initials.

Setup runs from 4:00 p.m. to 5:45 p.m.; bottled drinks must stay on the hallway shelf outside the gallery.

Sincerely,
K. Nagai
passage.translation: 地域アーカイブ・ボランティア窓口の永井から高校歴史部員への連絡。金曜の市民ギャラリー展示「商店街の暮らし 1960〜1990」の設営協力へのお礼。住民から60点以上の当時の家族写真や商店の帳簿を借用しているため、午後の設営では慎重な扱いが不可欠。実物の写真や紙の帳簿に触れる際は必ず作業台の清潔な白い綿手袋を着用すること（素手の皮脂は目に見えない跡を残し、古い銀塩写真の上で徐々に茶色く変色するため）。スマートフォンを操作したりボールペンでメモを書いたりする際は、インクや画面の汚れが資料に移らないよう一度手袋を外すこと。各展示ケースには実物資料と店主インタビューに基づく紹介カードを並べるが、ケースに入れる前に緑のバインダーの同意書を確認し、貸出者がフルネーム掲載を希望したかイニシャル表記を希望したか確かめること。設営は午後4時〜5時45分で、ペットボトル飲料はギャラリー外の廊下の棚に置くこと。

items.prompt: Why do students need to check the green binder before placing story cards in cases?
choices: To see which photographs can be given away for free.
To calculate how much rent each shopkeeper owes.
To verify whether each resident wanted their full name or only initials shown.
To find the Wi-Fi password for the civic gallery.
items.explanation: 貸出者がフルネームでの掲載を望んだかイニシャル表記のみを望んだか、同意書で確認するため。
distractorReasons: 無料配布ではない。
家賃計算ではない。
第3段落の指示と一致。
Wi-Fiパスワードではない。
items.translation: 紹介カードをケースに入れる前に緑のバインダーを確認する必要があるのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: Why were hospital gardens often removed during the late twentieth century?
choices: Doctors believed green leaves spread winter colds.
City laws banned trees within one kilometer of clinics.
Patients refused to look out windows after surgery.
Hospitals focused on compact indoor efficiency and used outdoor space for parking or new wings.
items.explanation: 空調の効いた高効率な建物が優先され、かつての庭が駐車場や増築検査棟に転用されたため。

法律で樹木禁止とはない。
患者が窓を見るのを拒んだとはない。
第1段落の説明と一致。
items.translation: 20世紀後半に病院の庭園がしばしば取り壊されたのはなぜですか。

passage.title: How Hospital Courtyards Support Recovery
passage.text:
For much of the late twentieth century, hospital architecture prioritized compact efficiency: air-conditioned towers with short walking distances for staff, wipe-clean corridors, and sealed windows. Courtyards and gardens, once common around older infirmaries, were often paved over for parking or extra diagnostic wings. Over the past twenty years, however, medical planners have been bringing greenery back into the heart of hospital buildings—not merely as decoration, but as a practical aid to care.

Interest grew after clinical studies compared patients recovering from similar surgeries in rooms facing trees with those facing blank brick walls. Patients with a view of foliage tended to report less discomfort, sleep more steadily, and transition home slightly sooner. Subsequent research in rehabilitation wards showed that accessible outdoor courtyards motivated patients learning to walk again: reaching a sunlit bench beside seasonal flowers felt like a meaningful goal compared with counting tiles down a fluorescent hallway.

Designing an effective hospital garden requires far more care than planting a public park. Paths must be wide, level, and glare-free so IV poles and wheelchairs roll without jolting. Strongly scented lilies or heavy pollen-producing trees can bother patients sensitive to smells after chemotherapy, so landscape architects favor gentle textures, rustling bamboo, trickling water, and herbs whose fragrance appears only when someone chooses to brush a leaf. Shaded seating pockets also give family members and nurses a quiet five-minute refuge to reset emotionally between difficult conversations.

Skeptics understandably ask whether garden maintenance belongs in tight healthcare budgets. Yet hospitals that track staff turnover and visitor satisfaction increasingly treat well-designed courtyards as shared infrastructure. When nurses have a calm place to step outside on break and patients move more willingly during physical therapy, modest landscaping pays quiet returns across the whole institution.
passage.translation: 20世紀後半の多くの期間、病院建築では職員の動線の短さや清掃しやすい廊下、密閉窓を備えた空調ビルといった効率性が最優先され、かつて見られた中庭や庭園は駐車場や検査棟に変わりました。しかし過去20年で、単なる飾りではなくケアを支える実用的な空間として緑を建物内部へ戻す動きが広がっています。きっかけは同様の手術後の患者を比較した臨床研究で、木々が見える病室の患者のほうがレンガ壁向きの患者より不快感が少なく睡眠も安定する傾向が示されました。リハビリ病棟でも、蛍光灯の廊下のタイルを数えて歩くより季節の花のそばの日当たりのよいベンチを目指すほうが歩行訓練の意欲が高まりました。もっとも医療庭園の設計には公園以上の配慮が要ります。点滴台や車いすが揺れない平らで反射の少ない通路が不可欠で、化学療法後でにおいに敏感な患者のため香りの強いユリや花粉の多い木は避け、触れたときだけ香るハーブや笹の音、せせらぎが選ばれます。木陰のベンチは家族や看護師が気持ちを整える5分間の拠り所にもなり、職員の定着や患者の前向きなリハビリを通じて病院全体を支える基盤となっています。

items.prompt: How did outdoor courtyards help patients in rehabilitation wards?
choices: They allowed patients to skip physical therapy altogether.
Walking to a sunny bench by flowers gave patients a more motivating goal than a plain hallway.
Courtyards had escalators that carried wheelchairs automatically.
Patients grew all the vegetables served in the hospital cafeteria.
items.explanation: 蛍光灯の廊下のタイルを数えるのに比べ、季節の花のそばの陽だまりのベンチまで歩くことが意味のある目標となり意欲を高めた。
distractorReasons: リハビリを休めるのではない。
第2段落後半の記述と一致。
自動エスカレーターの話はない。
給食用の全野菜栽培ではない。
items.translation: 屋外の中庭はリハビリ病棟の患者をどのように助けましたか。

items.prompt: Why do hospital garden designers avoid strongly scented flowers and heavy pollen trees?
choices: They attract bears into city centers.
They cost ten times more than bamboo.
Strong odors and pollen can trouble sensitive patients, such as those undergoing chemotherapy.
Nurses are not allowed to smell flowers on break.
items.explanation: 化学療法後などでにおいに敏感な患者や花粉に弱い人の負担になるため、触れたときだけ香るハーブや笹などが選ばれる。
distractorReasons: クマを呼ぶからではない。
10倍高いからではない。
第3段落の理由と一致。
看護師の規則ではない。
items.translation: 病院庭園の設計者が香りの強すぎる花や花粉の多い木を避けるのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: Besides patients, who else benefits directly from shaded courtyard seating?
choices: Delivery truck drivers parking inside the garden.

Ticket sellers collecting admission fees at the gate.
items.explanation: 難しい話し合いの合間などに気持ちを落ち着ける5分間の静かな居場所を必要とする家族や看護師。
distractorReasons: トラックは庭に駐車しない。
第3段落末・第4段落の記述と一致。
入場料徴収の話はない。
騒音機械テストではない。
items.translation: 患者のほかに、木陰の中庭ベンチから直接恩恵を受けるのは誰ですか。

As a way to replace all surgical equipment.
As a wasteful luxury that should be cut first.
As a temporary trend suitable only for tropical islands.

手術機器の代替ではない。
真っ先に削る無駄とは逆。
熱帯の島限定ではない。
items.translation: よく設計された中庭の維持費について、近年の病院はどう捉えるようになっていますか。

passage.title: Why Libraries Lend Musical Instruments and Tools
passage.text:
Public libraries built their reputation on lending books, magazines, and music recordings. Over the past decade, however, hundreds of municipal libraries have added an unexpected shelf near the circulation desk—a "library of things" stocked with sewing machines, ukuleles, stargazing telescopes, and household tool kits.

The idea addresses a practical pattern of modern living. Many apartment dwellers want to mend a torn curtain once a year, test whether a child enjoys playing an instrument before buying one, or observe a lunar eclipse on a single clear evening. Buying, storing, and maintaining specialized equipment for occasional use strains both family budgets and closet space. (18), sharing sturdy items across a neighborhood keeps dozens of rarely used machines from gathering dust.

Running such a collection takes planning, of course. Librarians work with local repair volunteers to check returned drills and tune stringed instruments between loans, and borrowers sign a brief safety checklist. Surprisingly, damage rates have stayed low; patrons treat shared equipment with care because (19).

Beyond saving money, tool and instrument lending has brought new faces through library doors. Hands-on items show that a public library is ultimately dedicated to (20), whatever form learning happens to take.
passage.translation: 公共図書館は本や雑誌、音楽ソフトの貸出で信頼を築いてきましたが、ここ10年で貸出カウンター近くにミシンやウクレレ、天体望遠鏡、家庭用工具セットを並べる「モノの図書館」を設ける自治体が増えています。背景には現代の暮らしの実情があります。集合住宅に暮らす人の多くは、年に一度カーテンのほつれを直したり、購入前に子どもが楽器を楽しめるか試したり、晴れた一晩だけ月食を観察したりしたいと考えます。たまにしか使わない専門用具を各家庭が購入・保管するのは家計にも収納にも負担です。(18)、丈夫な道具を地域で共有すれば、めったに使われない何十台もの機材が埃をかぶらずに済みます。返却された電動ドリルの点検や弦楽器の調律には地域の修理ボランティアが協力し、利用者も簡単な安全確認票に署名しますが、破損率は驚くほど低く抑えられています。(19)からです。節約以上に、新しい来館者層を呼び込んだことも大きな成果であり、実物の貸出は公共図書館の本来の使命が(20)にあることを示しています。

passage.title: How Ferries Cut Fuel Use with Wind Rotor Sails
passage.text:
When people picture wind-powered ships, they usually imagine canvas sails billowing from wooden masts. Modern car ferries and cargo vessels look nothing like nineteenth-century clippers, yet a growing number now carry tall, spinning white cylinders on their decks to capture wind energy alongside regular engines.

These cylinders, known as rotor sails, rely on a physical principle familiar to baseball pitchers and tennis players. When a motor spins the vertical cylinder slowly in a crosswind, air speeds up on one side of the drum and slows down on the other. The resulting pressure difference pushes the ship forward at right angles to the wind. Because the motor spinning the cylinder uses only a tiny fraction of the thrust generated, ferries crossing windy straits can throttle back their main diesel engines. (21), operators on North Sea routes have recorded fuel savings of eight to fifteen percent.

Unlike fabric sails, rotor cylinders require no extra deck crew to hoist or fold when squalls hit; bridge computers adjust rotation speed automatically as wind direction changes. (22), some designs tilt flat onto the deck at the push of a button so the ship can pass safely beneath low harbor bridges.

Rotor sails cannot power a heavy ferry on calm days, nor are they meant to work alone. Rather, combining aerodynamic physics with modern automation gives shipping lines (23) while cleaner fuels are still scaling up.
passage.translation: 風で進む船と聞くと木のマストに張られた布の帆を思い浮かべがちですが、現代のカーフェリーや貨物船の中には、通常のエンジンと併用して風の力を得るため、甲板に背の高い白い回転円筒を立てる船が増えています。「ローターセイル」と呼ばれるこの円筒は野球の変化球やテニスと同じ物理原理を利用します。横風の中で垂直な円筒をモーターでゆっくり回転させると、片側の気流が速まり反対側が遅くなって気圧差が生まれ、船を前へ押し出す推力が働きます。回転用モーターが使う電力は生まれる推力のごく一部にすぎないため、風の強い海峡を渡るフェリーは主ディーゼルエンジンの出力を絞ることができます。(21)、北海航路では8〜15％の燃料削減が記録されています。布の帆と違って突風のたびに甲板員が上げ下ろしする必要はなく、風向きに応じて船橋のコンピュータが回転数を自動調整します。(22)、低い港の橋をくぐる際にはボタンひとつで甲板へ水平に倒せる設計もあります。無風の日には頼れませんが、空力と自動制御の組み合わせは次世代燃料が普及するまでの間に海運会社へ(23)をもたらしています。

passage.title: How Ferries Cut Fuel Use with Wind Rotor Sails
passage.text:
When people picture wind-powered ships, they usually imagine canvas sails billowing from wooden masts. Modern car ferries and cargo vessels look nothing like nineteenth-century clippers, yet a growing number now carry tall, spinning white cylinders on their decks to capture wind energy alongside regular engines.

These cylinders, known as rotor sails, rely on a physical principle familiar to baseball pitchers and tennis players. When a motor spins the vertical cylinder slowly in a crosswind, air speeds up on one side of the drum and slows down on the other. The resulting pressure difference pushes the ship forward at right angles to the wind. Because the motor spinning the cylinder uses only a tiny fraction of the thrust generated, ferries crossing windy straits can throttle back their main diesel engines. (21), operators on North Sea routes have recorded fuel savings of eight to fifteen percent.

Unlike fabric sails, rotor cylinders require no extra deck crew to hoist or fold when squalls hit; bridge computers adjust rotation speed automatically as wind direction changes. (22), some designs tilt flat onto the deck at the push of a button so the ship can pass safely beneath low harbor bridges.

Rotor sails cannot power a heavy ferry on calm days, nor are they meant to work alone. Rather, combining aerodynamic physics with modern automation gives shipping lines (23) while cleaner fuels are still scaling up.

passage.title: Instructions for the Saturday Wetland Bird Count
passage.text:
From: M. Kurata, Bird Conservation Group
To: Student Survey Volunteers
Subject: Observation points and quiet-zone rules for Saturday

Dear student volunteers,
Thank you for joining our winter waterfowl count at Ashihara Marsh this Saturday morning. Migratory ducks and wild geese feed near the reed beds soon after sunrise, so we will meet at the south parking shelter at 6:40 a.m. and walk to our four wooden hides in small groups.

Each group includes an experienced spotter with a high-powered scope; your job is to record species counts every fifteen minutes on the waterproof clipboards provided. Please switch your phones to silent mode and turn screen brightness all the way down before entering a hide, as sudden flashes of white light through the viewing slots can startle resting flocks.

Because two hides stand over shallow water, icy breezes come up through the floorboards. Wear wool socks—two thin pairs trap more warmth than one tight thick pair—and bring a thermos of warm drink if you like, though strongly scented soup should wait until we return to the shelter at 9:30 a.m.

Best regards,
M. Kurata
passage.translation: 野鳥保全グループの倉田から生徒調査ボランティアへの連絡。今週土曜朝の芦原（Ashihara）湿原での冬のカモ・ガン類生息数調査の案内。渡り鳥は日の出直後にヨシ原近くで採食するため、午前6時40分に南駐車場のあずまやに集合し少人数で4つの木製観察小屋へ向かう。各班には高倍率スコープを持った熟練調査員がつき、生徒は配布される防水バインダーに15分ごとの種別個体数を記録する。観察窓から白い光が漏れると休んでいる群れを驚かせるため、小屋に入る前に携帯電話をマナーモードにし画面の明るさを最小まで下げること。2つの小屋は浅い水上に建っており床板の隙間から冷たい風が上がるためウールの靴下（きつい厚手1枚より薄手2枚重ねのほうが暖かい）を履き、必要なら保温水筒で温かい飲み物を持参してよいが、匂いの強いスープは9時30分にあずまやへ戻るまで控えること。

passage.title: Why Cities Are Uncovering Buried Streams
passage.text:
Beneath the asphalt of almost every major city flow dozens of forgotten brooks and small rivers. During periods of rapid urban growth in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, engineers routinely encased neighborhood streams in underground concrete pipes—known as culverts—to gain flat land for roads, prevent rubbish dumping, and move rainwater out of town as fast as possible. Out of sight, these waterways vanished from maps and local memory alike.

Climate pressures and aging pipes are now prompting municipalities to reverse course through a practice called "daylighting"—lifting buried streams back into open air. Ironically, the old concrete channels designed to prevent localized puddles often worsen flooding downstream during intense modern cloudbursts. Smooth underground pipes shoot storm runoff forward all at once, overwhelming river junctions below. An open channel lined with stones, curves, and terraced banks slows the water down and gives high flows safe room to spread.

Bringing water back to the surface transforms urban neighborhoods in quieter months as well. Shaded streamside paths run several degrees cooler than surrounding streets on August afternoons, while riffles oxygenate the water enough for dragonflies, minnows, and herons to return within a remarkably short time. Shopkeepers along famous daylighting projects—from Seoul to Zurich—have seen foot traffic rise as once-noisy traffic lanes become pleasant places to linger.

Daylighting is not feasible everywhere, of course. Where apartment blocks or subway tunnels sit directly atop a culvert, rerouting the stream through an adjacent park strip or widening parallel greenways may be the only practical option, and upstream street runoff must be filtered through gravel beds before entering the open brook.

Even modest stretches of uncovered water remind residents that a city is built atop living geography rather than a blank concrete slab.

passage.title: Why Cities Are Uncovering Buried Streams
passage.text:
Beneath the asphalt of almost every major city flow dozens of forgotten brooks and small rivers. During periods of rapid urban growth in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, engineers routinely encased neighborhood streams in underground concrete pipes—known as culverts—to gain flat land for roads, prevent rubbish dumping, and move rainwater out of town as fast as possible. Out of sight, these waterways vanished from maps and local memory alike.

Climate pressures and aging pipes are now prompting municipalities to reverse course through a practice called "daylighting"—lifting buried streams back into open air. Ironically, the old concrete channels designed to prevent localized puddles often worsen flooding downstream during intense modern cloudbursts. Smooth underground pipes shoot storm runoff forward all at once, overwhelming river junctions below. An open channel lined with stones, curves, and terraced banks slows the water down and gives high flows safe room to spread.

Bringing water back to the surface transforms urban neighborhoods in quieter months as well. Shaded streamside paths run several degrees cooler than surrounding streets on August afternoons, while riffles oxygenate the water enough for dragonflies, minnows, and herons to return within a remarkably short time. Shopkeepers along famous daylighting projects—from Seoul to Zurich—have seen foot traffic rise as once-noisy traffic lanes become pleasant places to linger.

Daylighting is not feasible everywhere, of course. Where apartment blocks or subway tunnels sit directly atop a culvert, rerouting the stream through an adjacent park strip or widening parallel greenways may be the only practical option, and upstream street runoff must be filtered through gravel beds before entering the open brook.

passage.title: Why Groceries Use Curved Shopping Cart Tracks on Ramps
passage.text:
Multi-story supermarkets in compact city neighborhoods face a logistical puzzle: how can customers move heavy carts full of milk, rice, and vegetables smoothly between floors? Ordinary passenger elevators fill up after just two or three carts, while regular stepped escalators cannot carry wheeled baskets safely.

Many urban stores solve this with inclined moving walkways—flat, grooved metal belts that climb slowly from floor to floor. At first glance, keeping a thirty-kilogram cart from rolling backward down a twelve-degree slope looks risky, especially if a shopper lets go of the handle to check a shopping list. Yet no motors or handbrakes are attached to the carts themselves. (18), the secret lies in the precise spacing of the cart's wheels and the narrow slots cut into the walkway floor.

As a cart rolls onto the ramp, its thin rubber tires drop neatly between raised metal ribs, allowing the slightly wider brake pads beside each wheel to rest directly on top of the ribs. Friction between those pads and the metal surface locks the cart firmly in place until it reaches the flat landing at the top, where a gentle comb plate lifts the tires out again. (19), shoppers can ride hands-free without fear of a runaway basket.

Because every cart wheel must match the walkway's rib width to the millimeter, stores cannot mix carts from different manufacturers. This quiet mechanical partnership shows how (20).
passage.translation: 都市部の手狭な地域にある複数階建てのスーパーマーケットには、牛乳や米、野菜を積んだ重いカートをどうやって階から階へ安全に運ぶかという課題があります。普通のエレベーターはカートが2〜3台入れば満員になり、段差のある通常のエスカレーターには車輪付きのかごを乗せられません。そこで多くの都市型店舗が導入しているのが、溝のついた平らな金属ベルトがゆっくり上り下りする斜行式の動く歩道（オートスロープ）です。買い物客がメモを見るため手を離したとき、傾斜12度の坂で30キロのカートが後ろへ転がり落ちないのは不思議に見えますが、カート自体にモーターやハンドブレーキはついていません。(18)、その秘密はカートの車輪幅と床面の細い溝の精密な寸法にあります。スロープに乗ると細いゴムタイヤが金属のリブ（突起）の間に落ち込み、車輪横のわずかに幅広いブレーキパッドがリブの上に密着して摩擦でカートを固定し、終端の平らな床に着くとくし状の板がタイヤを持ち上げて解放します。(19)、買い物客はカートが暴走する心配なく手放しでも乗っていられます。ミリ単位の一致が必要なため他社製カートは混ぜられませんが、この静かな機械的連携は(20)ことを示しています。

passage.title: Why Groceries Use Curved Shopping Cart Tracks on Ramps
passage.text:
Multi-story supermarkets in compact city neighborhoods face a logistical puzzle: how can customers move heavy carts full of milk, rice, and vegetables smoothly between floors? Ordinary passenger elevators fill up after just two or three carts, while regular stepped escalators cannot carry wheeled baskets safely.

Many urban stores solve this with inclined moving walkways—flat, grooved metal belts that climb slowly from floor to floor. At first glance, keeping a thirty-kilogram cart from rolling backward down a twelve-degree slope looks risky, especially if a shopper lets go of the handle to check a shopping list. Yet no motors or handbrakes are attached to the carts themselves. (18), the secret lies in the precise spacing of the cart's wheels and the narrow slots cut into the walkway floor.

As a cart rolls onto the ramp, its thin rubber tires drop neatly between raised metal ribs, allowing the slightly wider brake pads beside each wheel to rest directly on top of the ribs. Friction between those pads and the metal surface locks the cart firmly in place until it reaches the flat landing at the top, where a gentle comb plate lifts the tires out again. (19), shoppers can ride hands-free without fear of a runaway basket.

Because every cart wheel must match the walkway's rib width to the millimeter, stores cannot mix carts from different manufacturers. This quiet mechanical partnership shows how (20).

passage.title: How Oyster Reefs Calm Coastal Waves
passage.text:
When coastal towns think about defending harbors and roads against storm waves, concrete seawalls usually come to mind first. Massive walls block water effectively at the start, yet waves crashing against vertical concrete scour away sand at the base, requiring expensive repairs decade after decade. Over time, concrete barriers also replace shallow tidal zones where young fish once sheltered.

Marine engineers and ecologists have been testing a living complement in sheltered bays: artificial reefs seeded with native oysters. Young oysters attach themselves to shells or limestone blocks on the seafloor, cementing new layers atop old ones year after year. Unlike a rigid wall that wears down after construction, a healthy oyster reef actually grows denser and slightly taller as sea levels inch upward. (21), its rough, uneven surface breaks the energy of incoming waves before they strike the shore.

Water quality improves alongside shoreline stability. A single adult oyster filters dozens of liters of murky bay water a day, removing excess algae so sunlight can reach underwater eelgrass meadows again. (22), crabs, shrimp, and juvenile rockfish return to hide in the maze of shells.

Oyster reefs cannot replace concrete barriers along open ocean cliffs hit by giant typhoons. In calm estuaries and inner harbors, however, combining modest stone sills with living shell beds offers (23).
passage.translation: 沿岸の町が高潮や波から港や道路を守る方法を考えるとき、まず思い浮かぶのはコンクリートの防潮堤です。巨大な壁は当初こそ水を効果的に食い止めますが、垂直なコンクリートに打ち寄せる波が根元の砂をえぐり取るため何十年も高額な補修が必要になり、稚魚が隠れていた浅瀬も失われがちです。そこで海洋技術者と生態学者が穏やかな湾内で試しているのが、在来のカキを定着させた人工礁（オイスターリーフ）です。海底の貝殻や石灰岩ブロックに付着した稚ガキは年々殻を積み重ねていき、建設後に劣化していく硬い壁とは異なり、海面がわずかに上昇しても自ら厚く高くなっていきます。(21)、そのゴツゴツした不均一な表面が岸に届く前に波のエネルギーを砕いて弱めます。さらに成体のカキ1個が1日に何十リットルもの濁った海水をろ過して余分な藻類を除くため海底のアマモ場に光が届くようになり、(22)、カニやエビ、メバルの稚魚が殻の迷路に隠れに戻ってきます。外洋の断崖ではコンクリート堤の代わりにはなりませんが、穏やかな河口や内湾では低い石組みと生きたカキ礁の組み合わせが(23)をもたらします。

passage.title: Borrowing Musical Scores from the Regional Archive
passage.text:
From: Prefectural Youth Orchestra Library
To: Section Leaders
Subject: Handling rules for borrowed orchestral sheet music

Dear section leaders,
Sheet music folders for our winter symphony program are ready to pick up starting tomorrow afternoon. Because two of the pieces are rented from a national music publisher under a strict contract, please share these handling rules with everyone in your instrument section before the first rehearsal.

Players may write bowings, breath marks, and fingerings ONLY with soft 2B or 4B lead pencils. Ballpoint pens, highlighters, and erasable friction pens are strictly forbidden—friction-pen ink can reappear in cold delivery trucks even after being rubbed out, resulting in heavy replacement fines from the publisher.

Do not remove staples or tape loose pages together. If a page tear makes turning difficult on the stand, bring the folder to the orchestra librarian before rehearsal so archival paper tape can be applied cleanly. All numbered folders must be returned with markings fully erased within three days after the December concert.

Thank you for your care,
M. Kurosawa, Orchestra Librarian
passage.translation: 県青少年オーケストラ楽譜室（黒澤）からパートリーダーへの連絡。冬の交響曲プログラムの楽譜フォルダが明日の午後から受け取り可能になる。うち2曲は全国の楽譜出版社からの厳格な契約に基づくレンタル譜であるため、初回練習前にパート全員へ取扱規則を共有してほしい。弓順・ブレス記号・指番号の書き込みは柔らかい2Bまたは4Bの黒鉛筆のみ可。ボールペン、蛍光ペン、消せるフリクションペンは厳禁（フリクションのインクは消したあとでも低温の配送トラック内で浮き出ることがあり、出版社から高額な弁償金が請求される）。ホチキスを外したりページをテープで貼り合わせたりしないこと。破れて譜面台でめくりにくい場合は練習前にライブラリアンへ持参すれば保存用紙テープで補修する。番号付きフォルダはすべて12月の演奏会後3日以内に書き込みを完全に消して返却すること。

passage.title: Why Mapmakers Deliberately Straightened Subway Lines
passage.text:
Early transit maps of major cities in the 1910s and 1920s tried faithfully to show every twist of a railway line atop an accurate street map. As networks expanded, however, the results became nearly unreadable. Central business districts were crammed with tiny overlapping station names, while long suburban branches stretched off the edges of pocket folders.

In 1931, an electrical engineering draftsman named Harry Beck noticed something crucial while sketching London's Underground during a layoff. Once passengers descend beneath the pavement, they cannot see curving streets or rivers anyway; what they really need to know is which line to board, how many stops remain, and where two lines intersect. Drawing inspiration from electrical circuit diagrams—where wires are arranged neatly at horizontal, vertical, and forty-five-degree angles regardless of physical length—Beck compressed distant suburbs and enlarged the crowded center.

passage.title: Why Airport Carpets Are Quieter Than Terminal Tiles
passage.text:
Travelers rushing between airport gates with wheeled carry-on bags quickly feel the difference underfoot when polished stone hallways give way to low-pile carpet near seating areas. While stone and terrazzo tiles are easy to mop and let suitcase wheels glide effortlessly, many international terminals deliberately install wide stretches of patterned carpet around gates and quiet lounges.

Noise control is the primary reason. An airport concourse with glass walls and high metal ceilings acts like an echo chamber: announcements, rolling luggage, and hundreds of conversations bounce endlessly unless soft materials absorb sound waves. Stepping onto carpet immediately lowers ambient noise by several decibels, which reduces travel stress and makes boarding calls easier to hear. (18), softer flooring encourages passengers waiting for delayed flights to speak more quietly without even realizing it.

Designers also choose carpet patterns with surprising care. Subtle geometric weaves in blues, grays, or local landscape motifs hide coffee spills and wheel marks between nightly cleanings while making vast waiting halls feel more like calm living rooms. Heavy luggage carts do require slightly more force to push across carpet, however. (19), modern terminals lay smooth hard-stone "highways" down the center of main corridors and reserve carpet for gate seating zones.

Combining hard travel lanes with soft waiting islands shows how public architecture can (20).
passage.translation: キャスター付きのスーツケースを引いて空港の搭乗口へ向かう旅行者は、磨かれた石畳の通路から待合エリアの毛足の短いカーペットへ入った瞬間、足元の違いにすぐ気づきます。石やテラゾーの床はモップ掛けしやすく車輪も軽く転がりますが、多くの国際空港ターミナルでは搭乗口周辺やラウンジにあえて広い柄入りカーペットを敷いています。最大の理由は防音です。ガラス壁と高い金属天井を持つコンコースは音が反響しやすく、柔らかい素材が音波を吸収しないと館内放送や車輪の音、何百人もの話し声が際限なく響いてしまいます。カーペットに入ると周囲の騒音が数デシベル下がり、移動のストレスが和らぐうえ搭乗案内も聞き取りやすくなります。(18)、柔らかい床は遅延便を待つ乗客が無意識のうちに声を落として話す効果も生みます。柄選びにも工夫があり、青や灰色の繊細な幾何学模様がコーヒーの染みや車輪跡を目立たなくしつつ広い待合空間に落ち着きを与えます。もっとも重い手荷物カートはカーペット上では押しにくいため、(19)、現代のターミナルは主要通路の中央に滑らかな石畳の「幹線」を通し、カーペットは座席周辺に配しています。硬い移動レーンと柔らかい待機ゾーンの組み合わせは、公共建築がいかに(20)かを示しています。

passage.title: How Bakeries Reuse Unsold Bread Without Waste
passage.text:
Artisan bakeries face a daily dilemma: customers expect shelves to offer a reasonable choice of loaves even at five in the afternoon, yet bread baked without preservatives loses its crisp crust by the next morning. Bake too little, and afternoon commuters leave disappointed; bake a safety margin, and unsold loaves pile up at closing time.

Discounting bread during the final hour helps, and food banks gladly collect part of the surplus. Even so, irregular weather—such as a sudden downpour at four o'clock—can leave dozens of baguettes untouched. Rather than throwing good grain away, traditional and modern bakers alike have developed tasty second lives for day-old bread. Sliced baguettes brushed with almond cream and baked twice become crisp almond bostock or rusks that stay fresh for weeks. (21), hearth loaves ground into fine crumbs can replace up to a quarter of the fresh flour in the next day's sourdough batch, adding deep toasted aroma.

Researchers studying food-fermentation cycles have taken reuse one step further. Some craft beverage makers partner with neighborhood bakeries to brew non-alcoholic malt drinks and kvass-style sodas from surplus crusts. (22), bakeries cut disposal costs while gaining a distinctive local drink to sell beside lunch sandwiches.

Turning yesterday's loaves into tomorrow's ingredients proves that (23).
passage.translation: こだわりのパン屋は毎日ジレンマに直面します。夕方5時に来店する客にも選べるだけの品ぞろえが求められる一方、保存料を使わないパンは翌朝には皮の香ばしさが失われてしまいます。少なく焼けば夕方の通勤客をがっかりさせ、余裕をもって焼けば閉店時に売れ残りが出ます。閉店1時間前の値引きやフードバンクへの寄付も役立ちますが、夕方4時の急な土砂降りなど天候次第では何十本ものバゲットが残ることもあります。そこで伝統と現代の知恵を合わせ、1日経ったパンにおいしい第二の命を与える工夫が広がっています。スライスしたバゲットにアーモンドクリームを塗って二度焼きすれば数週間日持ちするボストックやラスクになり、(21)、ハード系パンを細かく砕いたパン粉を翌日のサワードウ生地の粉の最大4分の1に置き換えれば深い香ばしさが加わります。さらに発酵研究を応用し、地域の飲料工房と組んで余ったパンの耳からノンアルコールの麦芽飲料やクワス風ソーダを醸造する取り組みも進んでおり、(22)、パン屋は廃棄費用を減らしつつサンドイッチと一緒に売れる個性的な地元飲料を得られます。昨日のパンを明日の材料へ変える工夫は、(23)ことを証明しています。

distractorReasons: 焼く前に、ではない。

passage.title: Guidelines for the Inter-High Pottery Packing Day
passage.text:
From: Mr. Nagase, Art Club Advisor
To: Ceramic Section Members
Subject: Packing glazed works for Friday's exhibition van

Hello ceramic members,
The courier van for the Prefectural High School Art Exhibition will arrive at our loading bay at 8:15 a.m. this Friday. Because thirty fragile bowls, vases, and teapots must travel forty kilometers over mountain roads, we will pack every piece together after school on Thursday—do not pack your work alone during lunch break.

Each piece must follow the "double-box" rule: wrap your work in three layers of bubble wrap, place it inside a small inner carton cushioned with crumpled newspaper, and then set that inner carton inside a larger outer crate with five centimeters of padding on all sides. Never pack two ceramic pieces inside the same inner carton without a thick cardboard divider, even if they belong to a matching tea set; vibration on curves makes unseparated glazes chip against each other.

passage.title: Why Ancient Roman Sea Concrete Lasted Millennia
passage.text:
Modern steel-reinforced concrete is the backbone of bridges, ports, and high-rises around the world. Strong as it is on land, ordinary Portland cement concrete struggles in saltwater: within fifty to eighty years, seawater seeps through microscopic pores, rusts the internal steel bars, and causes the surrounding stone to crack and flake. Walk along Italian harbors built two thousand years ago, however, and you can still stand on unreinforced Roman concrete breakwaters that have endured pounding Mediterranean waves since antiquity.

For centuries, historians knew from ancient texts that Roman builders mixed volcanic ash from the Bay of Naples with lime and seawater, then packed the mortar around chunks of volcanic rock. Yet only recently did mineralogists using high-energy X-ray beams uncover the chemical secret inside surviving harbor cores. Where modern engineers strive to crush and blend lime until no lumps remain, Roman mortar contained tiny white mineral flecks once dismissed as sloppy mixing.

Far from being mistakes, those reactive lime flecks give the concrete a remarkable self-healing ability. Whenever wave stress opens a hairline crack, seawater trickles in, dissolves calcium from the lime flecks, and reacts with silica-rich volcanic ash to grow interlocking crystal plates right across the gap. Instead of widening into a structural failure, small fractures seal themselves and bind the rock tighter over decades.

Simply copying Roman recipes word for word will not suit every twenty-first-century project; Roman harbor concrete cured slowly and lacked the steel needed for slender highway spans. Even so, materials scientists are already adapting lime-and-volcanic-ash chemistry to design lower-carbon marine concretes that need fewer repairs.

Studying ancient harbors reminds engineers that durability sometimes comes from working with water's chemistry rather than fighting to keep every drop out.
passage.translation: 現代の鉄筋コンクリートは橋や港、高層ビルの要ですが、海水中では50〜80年ほどで微細な隙間から塩水が染み込んで内部の鉄筋を錆びさせ、ひび割れを起こしてしまいます。ところがイタリアの海岸を歩くと、鉄筋を一切使わずに2000年間も地中海の荒波に耐え抜いてきた古代ローマのコンクリート防波堤が今も残っています。ローマの技術者がナポリ湾の火山灰と石灰、海水を混ぜて火山岩を固めていたことは古文書から知られていましたが、高エネルギーX線で内部構造を解析した鉱物学者によって最近ようやく化学的秘密が解明されました。かつて「混ぜ方が雑だった証拠」と見なされていた小さな白い石灰の粒が、実は自己修復能力の鍵だったのです。波の負荷で髪の毛ほどのひびが入って海水が入り込むと、石灰粒から溶け出したカルシウムが火山灰のケイ素と反応し、隙間を埋める板状結晶が成長してひびを自然に塞ぎます。硬化が遅く細長い高架橋に必要な鉄筋も持たないため古代の配合をそのまま全てに使えるわけではありませんが、補修回数と炭素排出を抑えた新しい海洋コンクリートの開発にすでに活かされています。

items.prompt: How had researchers previously misinterpreted the tiny white lime flecks in Roman mortar?

As fragments of rusted iron tools.
items.explanation: tiny white mineral flecks once dismissed as sloppy mixing（かつては雑な混合によるムラだと見過ごされていた）。
distractorReasons: 装飾用の真珠ではない。
第2段落末の記述と一致。

鉄製道具の破片ではない。
items.translation: 研究者たちは以前、ローマのモルタルに含まれる小さな白い石灰粒をどう誤解していましたか。

passage.title: Why Escalators Have Brushes Along Their Sides
passage.text:
Look down at the bottom edges of almost any subway or department-store escalator, and you will notice rows of stiff black nylon bristles sticking inward from both side panels. Many riders casually use them to dust off their shoes—or assume the brushes are there to sweep candy wrappers off the moving steps. In fact, engineers added skirt brushes after investigating a serious mechanical hazard.

Between each moving metal step and the stationary side wall sits a tiny gap just a few millimeters wide. Without a physical barrier, soft rubber rain boots, trailing coat drawstrings, or long shopping bags resting right against the wall can get pulled into that gap by friction as the steps descend. Once fabric or rubber wedges inside, the escalator must halt abruptly. (18), a subtle sensory warning was needed to keep feet a few centimeters toward the center.

Stiff nylon bristles solve the problem gently through human reflexes. Whenever a passenger's shoe or pant leg brushes against the bristles, the light tickling sensation prompts the person to shift inward automatically without looking down. (19), the bristles physically deflect loose shoelaces before they can reach the narrow metal clearance.

Safety authorities made side brushes mandatory on new escalators in many countries after injury rates dropped sharply in early trials. Sometimes the best engineering safeguard is not a loud alarm, but (20).
passage.translation: 地下鉄や百貨店のエスカレーターの足元を見ると、左右の側面パネルから硬い黒いナイロンブラシが内側へ向かって並んでいるのに気づきます。靴のほこりを払うためのもの、あるいは動く段の上のごみを掃くためのものと思う乗客もいますが、実際には深刻な巻き込み事故を調査した技術者が導入した安全装置です。動く金属製のステップと固定された側壁の間には数ミリのわずかな隙間があり、物理的な仕切りがないと、柔らかいゴム長靴やコートのひも、壁際に置いた長い買い物袋が摩擦で引き込まれ、急停止につながることがありました。(18)、足を数センチ内側へ離しておくためのさりげない感覚的な警告が必要だったのです。硬めのナイロン毛は人間の反射を利用して穏やかに問題を解決します。靴やズボンの裾がブラシに触れると、くすぐったい感触で足元を見なくても無意識に内側へ足をずらすようになり、(19)、ほどけた靴ひもが金属の隙間に届く前に物理的に跳ね返す役割も果たします。初期試験で事故が激減したことから多くの国で新設機に義務化されましたが、優れた安全設計とは大音量の警報ではなく(20)場合があるのです。

passage.title: How Ice Stupas Store Winter Water for Spring Crops
passage.text:
High in the cold desert valleys of Ladakh in northern India, farmers receive less than ten centimeters of rain a year. For centuries, villages depended on summer meltwater trickling down from mountain glaciers to irrigate barley, peas, and apricot trees. As smaller low-altitude glaciers have retreated, however, streams now run dry during critical planting weeks in April and May, only to surge later in July.

Building concrete reservoirs at four thousand meters is costly, and shallow ponds freeze solid or evaporate quickly in fierce high-altitude sun. In 2013, local engineer Sonam Wangchuk tested an ingenious geometric alternative: piping unused winter stream water downhill by gravity and spraying it upward into subzero night air. Freezing as it falls, the spray builds a towering cone of ice thirty meters tall, shaped like a traditional Buddhist monument or stupa. (21), a cone exposes far less surface area to spring sunshine per liter of ice than a flat pond does.

Because of that compact shape, an ice stupa melts slowly throughout April, May, and June—releasing steady trickles of water right when young barley shoots need moisture most. Local youths maintain the pipes without electric pumps, since height difference alone creates water pressure. (22), villages can store millions of liters of winter runoff using simple hardware-store pipes.

Ice stupas cannot replace glacier conservation on a global scale, yet they give mountain communities (23) while adapting to shifting snowmelt seasons.

passage.title: How Ice Stupas Store Winter Water for Spring Crops
passage.text:
High in the cold desert valleys of Ladakh in northern India, farmers receive less than ten centimeters of rain a year. For centuries, villages depended on summer meltwater trickling down from mountain glaciers to irrigate barley, peas, and apricot trees. As smaller low-altitude glaciers have retreated, however, streams now run dry during critical planting weeks in April and May, only to surge later in July.

Building concrete reservoirs at four thousand meters is costly, and shallow ponds freeze solid or evaporate quickly in fierce high-altitude sun. In 2013, local engineer Sonam Wangchuk tested an ingenious geometric alternative: piping unused winter stream water downhill by gravity and spraying it upward into subzero night air. Freezing as it falls, the spray builds a towering cone of ice thirty meters tall, shaped like a traditional Buddhist monument or stupa. (21), a cone exposes far less surface area to spring sunshine per liter of ice than a flat pond does.

Because of that compact shape, an ice stupa melts slowly throughout April, May, and June—releasing steady trickles of water right when young barley shoots need moisture most. Local youths maintain the pipes without electric pumps, since height difference alone creates water pressure. (22), villages can store millions of liters of winter runoff using simple hardware-store pipes.

Ice stupas cannot replace glacier conservation on a global scale, yet they give mountain communities (23) while adapting to shifting snowmelt seasons.

passage.title: Preparing Audio Files for the Regional Drama Contest
passage.text:
From: Stage Technical Desk, Civic Theater
To: High School Drama Club Sound Operators
Subject: Sound file format and backup rules for Sunday's contest

Dear sound operators,
We look forward to supporting your technical rehearsal and performance this Sunday. Every year, at least one school experiences a playback hiccup because of file settings, so please check these requirements before Friday.

Submit all music cues and sound effects on a USB flash drive formatted in FAT32 or exFAT, saved as uncompressed WAV files (48 kHz, 16-bit). Do not rely on smartphones, Bluetooth receivers, or streaming apps in the booth—theater concrete walls block cellular signals, and notification chimes or automatic system updates can interrupt a quiet dramatic scene.

Name each file starting with a three-digit cue number in performance order (for example, "001_rain_intro.wav", "002_doorbell.wav"). In addition, bring an audio CD or a second identical USB drive in a separate bag as an emergency backup.

Stage Technical Desk
passage.translation: 市民劇場・舞台技術デスクから高校演劇部音響担当者へのメール。今週日曜のリハーサルおよび本番に向け、毎年ファイル設定が原因の再生トラブルが起きるため金曜までに要件を確認してほしい。すべての音楽きっかけと効果音はFAT32またはexFAT形式のUSBメモリに非圧縮WAV形式（48kHz・16bit）で保存して提出すること。音響ブースではスマートフォン、Bluetooth受信機、ストリーミングアプリに頼らないこと（劇場のコンクリート壁は電波を遮り、通知音や自動更新が静かな場面を妨げる恐れがある）。ファイル名は上演順に3桁のキュー番号から始めること（例：001_rain_intro.wav）。さらに非常用バックアップとして、音楽CDまたは同じ内容の2本目のUSBメモリを別のかばんに入れて持参すること。

All files must have the exact same filename.

passage.title: How Seed Vaults Keep Crop Diversity Alive Underground
passage.text:
Walk through a modern supermarket, and the fruit and vegetable section looks wonderfully varied. Yet agricultural historians point out a quiet vulnerability behind that colorful display: globally, just nine plant species account for nearly two-thirds of all crop production, and farmers within each crop increasingly plant a handful of high-yielding commercial varieties. While uniform crops simplify harvesting and transport, genetic uniformity carries risk. If a new fungal disease or prolonged drought strikes a widely planted wheat or potato variety, entire regions can lose harvests simultaneously.

Over previous centuries, peasant farmers maintained thousands of local "landrace" varieties—grains and beans adapted to salty coastal soil, high mountain frost, or short desert rains. When farms switch to modern commercial seeds, those hardy older varieties can vanish within a single generation unless someone preserves viable seeds.

That is the mission of over a thousand seed banks worldwide, backed up by the Svalbard Global Seed Vault deep inside an Arctic mountain in Norway. Sealed in moisture-proof foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, orthodox seeds such as wheat, rice, and lentils slow their metabolism so dramatically that they remain capable of sprouting for decades or even centuries. Permafrost surrounding the Arctic rock tunnel provides natural refrigeration even if external power temporarily fails.

Even the coldest vault is not a "set-and-forget" museum, however. Seeds slowly lose vigor over time and must periodically be thawed, planted in soil, harvested fresh, and frozen anew. Moreover, tropical crops with moist, fleshy seeds—such as cacao, mango, and avocado—cannot survive standard freezing at all; scientists preserve their diversity in living field collections or ultra-cold liquid nitrogen.

Safeguarding ancient seeds is ultimately forward-looking work: traits hidden in an obscure mountain grain today may hold the exact drought resistance breeders need fifty years from now.
passage.translation: 現代のスーパーの青果売り場は一見豊かに見えますが、世界全体の作物生産の約3分の2はわずか9種の植物に集中しており、しかも収穫や輸送に便利な少数の高収量品種への均一化が進んでいます。遺伝的に均一な作物は、新しいカビ病や長期干ばつが発生した際に地域全体の収穫が一度に失われるリスクを抱えています。かつて各地の農家が塩害地や高地の霜、砂漠の短い雨に適応させてきた何千もの在来品種は、現代品種への切り替えで1世代のうちに消滅しかねません。それを守るのが世界1000以上の種子銀行と、ノルウェー北極圏の岩山深くにあるスヴァールバル世界種子貯蔵庫です。防湿ホイル袋に密封して氷点下18度で保管すると小麦や稲、レンズ豆などの種子は代謝が極限まで遅くなり、数十年から数世紀にわたり発芽力を保てるうえ、周囲の永久凍土が停電時にも自然な保冷材となります。もっとも種子も時間とともに活力が落ちるため定期的な栽培更新が必要であり、カカオやマンゴー、アボカドのように水分の多い熱帯作物の種子は通常の冷凍に耐えられないため圃場保存や液体窒素が使われます。古い種子を守ることは、50年後の品種改良に必要な耐乾性など未来への備えそのものなのです。

passage.title: How Seed Vaults Keep Crop Diversity Alive Underground
passage.text:
Walk through a modern supermarket, and the fruit and vegetable section looks wonderfully varied. Yet agricultural historians point out a quiet vulnerability behind that colorful display: globally, just nine plant species account for nearly two-thirds of all crop production, and farmers within each crop increasingly plant a handful of high-yielding commercial varieties. While uniform crops simplify harvesting and transport, genetic uniformity carries risk. If a new fungal disease or prolonged drought strikes a widely planted wheat or potato variety, entire regions can lose harvests simultaneously.

Over previous centuries, peasant farmers maintained thousands of local "landrace" varieties—grains and beans adapted to salty coastal soil, high mountain frost, or short desert rains. When farms switch to modern commercial seeds, those hardy older varieties can vanish within a single generation unless someone preserves viable seeds.

That is the mission of over a thousand seed banks worldwide, backed up by the Svalbard Global Seed Vault deep inside an Arctic mountain in Norway. Sealed in moisture-proof foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, orthodox seeds such as wheat, rice, and lentils slow their metabolism so dramatically that they remain capable of sprouting for decades or even centuries. Permafrost surrounding the Arctic rock tunnel provides natural refrigeration even if external power temporarily fails.

Even the coldest vault is not a "set-and-forget" museum, however. Seeds slowly lose vigor over time and must periodically be thawed, planted in soil, harvested fresh, and frozen anew. Moreover, tropical crops with moist, fleshy seeds—such as cacao, mango, and avocado—cannot survive standard freezing at all; scientists preserve their diversity in living field collections or ultra-cold liquid nitrogen.

Safeguarding ancient seeds is ultimately forward-looking work: traits hidden in an obscure mountain grain today may hold the exact drought resistance breeders need fifty years from now.
passage.translation: 現代のスーパーの青果売り場は一見豊かに見えますが、世界全体の作物生産の約3分の2はわずか9種の植物に集中しており、しかも収穫や輸送に便利な少数の高収量品種への均一化が進んでいます。遺伝的に均一な作物は、新しいカビ病や長期干ばつが発生した際に地域全体の収穫が一度に失われるリスクを抱えています。かつて各地の農家が塩害地や高地の霜、砂漠の短い雨に適応させてきた何千もの在来品種は、現代品種への切り替えで1世代のうちに消滅しかねません。それを守るのが世界1000以上の種子銀行と、ノルウェー北極圏の岩山深くにあるスヴァールバル世界種子貯蔵庫です。防湿ホイル袋に密封して氷点下18度で保管すると小麦や稲、レンズ豆などの種子は代謝が極限まで遅くなり、数十年から数世紀にわたり発芽力を保てるうえ、周囲の永久凍土が停電時にも自然な保冷材となります。もっとも種子も時間とともに活力が落ちるため定期的な栽培更新が必要であり、カカオやマンゴー、アボカドのように水分の多い熱帯作物の種子は通常の冷凍に耐えられないため圃場保存や液体窒素が使われます。古い種子を守ることは、50年後の品種改良に必要な耐乾性など未来への備えそのものなのです。

items.prompt: Why can't crops like cacao, mango, and avocado be stored using standard minus-18-degree seed freezing?

distractorReasons: 食べられなくなったわけではない。

items.translation: カカオ、マンゴー、アボカドなどの作物が通常のマイナス18度種子冷凍で保存できないのはなぜですか。

passage.title: Why Escalator Brushes Line the Bottom of Every Side Skirt
passage.text:
Look down beside your shoes the next time you ride a station escalator, and you will see stiff black nylon bristles sticking out just above the moving metal steps. Playful commuters occasionally brush dust off their sneakers against them, assuming that shoe cleaning is why engineers put them there. In reality, those "skirt deflector brushes" are a mandatory safety device.

Escalator steps must glide past stationary side panels with a tiny clearance gap of a few millimeters. Without a physical reminder, passengers standing too close to the wall risk having soft rubber rain boots, long coat hems, or dangling shoelaces pulled into that narrow gap as steps fold flat at the landing. Stiff bristles tickle ankles gently the instant a foot drifts sideways. (18), riders instinctively shift half a step toward the safe center of the tread without even looking down.

Brushes help maintenance crews indirectly as well. Coins, ticket stubs, and small pebbles dropped from pockets bounce off the angled bristles instead of wedging into moving gears underneath. (19), mechanics inspect worn or bent brush strips every month just as carefully as brakes.

A row of simple nylon bristles illustrates how subtle tactile cues can (20).

passage.title: How Sponge Sidewalks Help Cities Handle Cloudbursts
passage.text:
Summer weather in many temperate cities has grown more uneven: weeks of dry heat are increasingly interrupted by intense one-hour cloudbursts that dump a month's rain in a single afternoon. Conventional streets paved from wall to wall with waterproof asphalt funnel every liter of rain straight into underground storm pipes. When pipes reach capacity, intersections flood while tree roots two meters below the pavement remain bone-dry.

To break this paradox, civil engineers are redesigning sidewalks as "rain gardens" and permeable pavements—part of what urban hydrologists call "sponge cities." Replacing solid concrete slabs along curb lanes with porous interlocking bricks, crushed-gravel trenches, and shallow planted basins lets rainwater soak straight into engineered soil beds beneath pedestrians' feet. (21), peak runoff entering municipal storm drains during a sudden downpour can drop by forty percent or more.

Storing moisture underground pays off weeks later when clear, hot weather returns. Street trees draw on that trapped soil water and release cool vapor through their leaves, lowering sidewalk temperatures noticeably. (22), gravel layers and plant roots filter brake dust and oil droplets out of street water before it seeps toward rivers.

Retrofitting every avenue takes years of utility coordination, so cities prioritize flood-prone low spots first. Step by step, porous streets turn sudden rain from an urban hazard into (23).
passage.translation: 多くの温帯都市で夏の天候が極端になり、何週間もの猛暑の合間に1か月分の雨が1時間で降るような局地的大雨が増えています。全面を水を通さないアスファルトで覆った従来の道路は雨水をすべて地下の排水管へ流し込むため、管が満杯になると交差点が冠水する一方、舗装の2メートル下にある街路樹の根はカラカラに乾いたままという矛盾が生じます。これを解消するため土木技術者が進めているのが「スポンジシティ」の一部である透水性歩道や雨水ます（レインガーデン）です。縁石沿いを穴あきブロックや砕石溝、浅い植栽帯に変えることで雨水が足元の土壌層へ直接しみ込み、(21)、急な豪雨時に下水管へ流れ込むピーク水量を40％以上減らせます。蓄えられた水分は晴天の猛暑が戻った際に街路樹の蒸散を助けて歩道を涼しくし、(22)、砂利層と根がブレーキ粉じんや油分をろ過してから川へ戻します。一歩ずつ透水化を進めることで、急な雨は都市の脅威から(23)へと変わっていきます。
